summary: For children aged 4-6, learning to order events in time and USE relational time language — first/next/last, before/after, the deictic terms today/yesterday/tomorrow, and morning/afternoon/evening. The hardest parts are the deictic terms (whose referent shifts as 'now' moves — tomorrow becomes today the next day) and the relational before/after. These are learned by talking through the daily routine, retelling sequences and stories, and anchoring words to concrete remembered and anticipated events — not by asking children to define words. Research describes deictic time words as acquired slowly and partially, so early slips are best treated as developmental rather than errors to drill.
misconceptions: Swaps yesterday and tomorrow (both used loosely for 'a day that isn't today')
Reverses before/after, or uses 'next' for the last thing
Ties morning/afternoon to particular activities rather than the time of day
Sequences by salience (the most exciting event first) rather than chronology

activities.title: Order the day and slide the 'today' marker
steps: Put pictures of the day's events — wake up, breakfast, school, bed — into chronological order.
Narrate the ordered sequence aloud using 'first… next… last' (e.g. 'first we wake up, next we have breakfast, last we go to bed').
The same drag-to-order can be used with story-sequencing picture cards: retell a familiar story in order, not only the daily routine, narrating it with first/next/last.

On a scrolling strip of consecutive days with a moveable 'today' marker (e.g. Tuesday–Wednesday–Thursday), start with 'today' on the MIDDLE day so both neighbours are visible, and say what happened yesterday (the day before) and what will happen tomorrow (the day after).

Slide the view forward one day, keeping 'today' on the middle slot: the day that was 'tomorrow' is now 'today', the day that was 'today' is now 'yesterday', the oldest day slides off and a new day comes into view ahead, so all three relative labels stay represented and keep re-pointing.
activities.insight: Yesterday and tomorrow are not interchangeable words for 'a day that isn't today' — they name a definite place relative to where 'now' sits, and they re-point as 'today' moves. Sequencing follows real chronology, not how exciting an event is.

activities.title: Talk through your day with a character
steps: Listen to a friendly character recount their own day in simple, concrete terms.
Tell the character what you did first and next in your own day.
Answer what you did yesterday and what you will do tomorrow, tied to real events you remember or expect.
Use 'morning' and 'afternoon' to say when something happened.
activities.insight: Time words are tools for talking about real, remembered and anticipated events — using them in authentic exchange is the goal, not reciting definitions.

activities.title: Name the parts of the day (naming scaffold)
steps: Tap parts of a daily-timeline picture to reveal labels — morning, afternoon, evening.
Match everyday activities to the time of day they usually happen.
Say when each shown activity happens using 'morning', 'afternoon' or 'evening'.
activities.insight: The day has named parts tied to the time of day, not to which single activity happens.

activities.title: Order a novel set of events
steps: Order a set of shuffled routine pictures (e.g. wake up, school, bed) into chronological order.
Narrate them with 'first', 'next', 'last' in true time order.

Answer a fresh-anchor deictic question, e.g. 'If today is Friday, is tomorrow a school day or the weekend?' (use this only where Saturday is a non-school weekend day for the child; otherwise choose days that match the child's own school week).
activities.insight: Demonstrate that sequencing and deictic reasoning transfer to a new, unrehearsed set of events and a fresh 'today' anchor.

checkQuestion: In the flow of talk about the day and week, listen for correct USE (never ask the child to define a word): (1) 'Tell me what you do in the morning, and what you do after that.' (2) Pointing at a day-strip: 'Today is Wednesday. What did we do yesterday? What will we do tomorrow?' (3) Show three shuffled routine pictures (wake up, school, bed): 'Put these in order and tell me what happens first, next and last.'
checkAnswer: Uses 'morning' and 'after' correctly while narrating; correctly names yesterday as the day before and tomorrow as the day after today; orders the three events and narrates them with first/next/last in true chronological order.
